name: Xia
summary: The first dynasty in Chinese tradition, associated with the Erlitou archaeological culture. Bronze ritual vessels, irrigation works and the earliest Chinese palace complexes mark this semi-legendary period.

fell.text: The last ruler Jie was overthrown by Tang of Shang, establishing the dynastic cycle.

name: Shang
summary: China's first historically confirmed dynasty with written records. Oracle bone divination, sophisticated bronze casting, wheeled chariots and the earliest form of Chinese writing characterize this Bronze Age civilization.

fell.text: King Wu of Zhou defeated the Shang at the Battle of Muye in 1046 BCE.

name: Western Zhou
summary: The early Zhou period when the royal court ruled from the western capital. Created the Mandate of Heaven concept, feudal system of enfeoffment, bronze ritual art and the foundations of Chinese philosophy.

fell.text: Quanrong nomads sacked the western capital; the court fled east to Luoyang.

name: Eastern Zhou
summary: The later Zhou period when royal power declined and rival states competed. Confucius, Laozi, Mencius and other philosophers flourished during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States eras, creating China's intellectual foundations.

fell.text: The Qin state conquered the last Zhou territories; the last Zhou king died in 256 BCE.

name: Qin
summary: China's first unified empire under Qin Shi Huang. Legalist philosophy, standardized writing and weights, the Terracotta Army and early sections of the Great Wall mark this brief but transformative dynasty.

fell.text: Popular rebellions following Qin Shi Huang's death led to the dynasty's collapse in 206 BCE.

name: Western Han
summary: The first half of the Han dynasty, establishing China as a major Eurasian power. Paper, the seismograph, the Silk Road and Confucian state orthodoxy emerged during this golden age.

fell.text: Wang Mang usurped the throne and established the Xin dynasty in 9 CE.

name: Xin
summary: The interregnum dynasty of Wang Mang, who attempted radical land reform and economic policies. His failed reforms and natural disasters led to widespread rebellion.

fell.text: Rebel forces captured Chang'an and executed Wang Mang in 23 CE.

name: Eastern Han
summary: The restored Han dynasty ruling from the eastern capital. Continued technological innovation, Buddhist introduction, expanded Silk Road trade and the compilation of major historical and scientific works.

fell.text: Emperor Xian abdicated to Cao Pi, ending the Han and beginning the Three Kingdoms period.

name: Cao Wei
summary: The most powerful of the Three Kingdoms, controlling northern China. Known for military innovation, administrative reforms and the poetry of the Cao family, though it fell to the Sima clan who founded the Jin.

fell.text: Sima Yan forced the last Wei emperor to abdicate and established the Jin dynasty.

name: Shu Han
summary: The smallest of the Three Kingdoms, ruling Sichuan under Liu Bei and his chancellor Zhuge Liang. Romanticized in literature as the legitimate Han successor, though militarily the weakest.

fell.text: Cao Wei forces conquered Shu Han in 263, capturing its capital Chengdu.

name: Eastern Wu
summary: The southernmost of the Three Kingdoms, controlling the Yangzi delta and southern coast. Known for naval power, maritime trade and the development of southern China under the Sun family.

fell.text: The Jin dynasty conquered Eastern Wu in 280, reunifying China.

name: Jin
summary: Briefly reunified China after the Three Kingdoms, but weak central authority led to the Wu Hu uprisings and division into Northern and Southern dynasties. Western Jin fell in 316; Eastern Jin ruled the south until 420.

fell.text: The last Jin emperor abdicated to Liu Yu, who founded the Liu Song dynasty.

name: Liu Song
summary: The first of the Southern Dynasties, ruling from Jiankang. Known for literary achievements, Buddhist patronage and the compilation of historical and scientific works during this period of cultural flowering.

fell.text: The last Liu Song emperor was deposed by Xiao Daocheng, who founded the Southern Qi dynasty.

name: Northern Wei
summary: The most successful of the Northern Dynasties, founded by the Tuoba clan of the Xianbei people. Promoted Buddhism, sinicization policies and created the equal-field system that influenced later dynasties.

fell.text: Internal conflicts split Northern Wei into Eastern Wei and Western Wei in 534.

name: Sui
summary: Reunified China after centuries of division, creating institutions that the Tang inherited. The Grand Canal connected north and south, but costly wars and building projects exhausted the dynasty.

fell.text: Emperor Yang was assassinated by his guards, and Li Yuan founded the Tang dynasty.

name: Tang
summary: China's golden age of cosmopolitan culture, Buddhist art, poetry and international trade. The Tang empire connected China to Central Asia, India and Persia through the Silk Road, producing figures like Li Bai, Du Fu and Empress Wu.

fell.text: The last Tang emperor was deposed by Zhu Wen, beginning the Five Dynasties period.

name: Later Liang
summary: The first of the Five Dynasties that ruled northern China between the Tang and Song. Founded by Zhu Wen, a former rebel turned Tang general who deposed the last Tang emperor.

fell.text: Later Tang forces conquered Later Liang and captured its capital in 923.

name: Song
summary: A period of economic revolution, technological innovation and cultural refinement. Printing, gunpowder, the compass and paper money transformed society, though military weakness led to the loss of northern China to the Jin in 1127.

fell.text: The last Song emperor died as Mongol forces conquered the final Song stronghold in 1279.

name: Goguryeo
summary: The largest of Korea's Three Kingdoms, controlling northern Korea and parts of Manchuria. Known for military prowess, Buddhist culture and distinctive tomb murals, though it fell to a Tang-Silla alliance.

fell.text: Goguryeo fell to a combined Tang Chinese and Silla Korean army after decades of warfare in 668.

name: Baekje
summary: A Korean kingdom known for maritime trade, refined Buddhist culture and artistic achievements. Baekje transmitted Buddhism and Chinese learning to Japan, playing a crucial role in East Asian cultural exchange.

fell.text: Silla forces allied with Tang China conquered Baekje in 660, capturing its capital Sabi.

name: Silla
summary: The smallest of Korea's Three Kingdoms that eventually unified the peninsula. Known for the bone-rank social system, gold crowns, Buddhist culture and the Hwarang warrior youth organization.

fell.text: The last Silla king surrendered to Goryeo in 935, ending the dynasty.

name: Balhae
summary: A multi-ethnic kingdom founded by former Goguryeo people in Manchuria. Known as the Flourishing State of the East, it maintained diplomatic and trade relations with Tang China, Japan and other regional powers.

fell.text: The Khitan Liao dynasty conquered Balhae in 926 after a surprise attack.

name: Goryeo
summary: A Korean dynasty that unified the peninsula and oversaw a golden age of Buddhist culture and artistic achievement. Famous for celadon ceramics, the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks and the world's first metal movable type printing.

fell.text: General Yi Seong-gye overthrew Goryeo and established the Joseon dynasty in 1392.

name: Joseon
summary: Korea's last dynasty, known for Neo-Confucian governance, the invention of Hangul alphabet by King Sejong, scientific instruments and the turtle ships of Admiral Yi Sun-sin.

fell.text: Joseon was reorganized as the Korean Empire in 1897 before Japanese annexation in 1910.

name: Yamato
summary: Early Japanese state centered in the Yamato region, characterized by large keyhole-shaped burial mounds and gradual unification under imperial authority. Adopted Chinese writing, Buddhism and administrative models.

fell.text: The establishment of a permanent capital at Nara in 710 marks the transition to the Nara period.

name: Nara
summary: Japan's first permanent capital period, modeled on Chinese Tang dynasty Chang'an. Buddhism flourished with state patronage, the Manyoshu poetry anthology compiled and the ritsuryo legal system established.

fell.text: The capital moved to Heian-kyo (Kyoto) in 794, beginning the Heian period.

name: Heian
summary: A golden age of Japanese court culture, producing The Tale of Genji, The Pillow Book and refined aesthetics. Aristocratic Fujiwara clan dominated politics while Buddhism developed distinctively Japanese forms like Pure Land and Tendai.

fell.text: The Minamoto clan defeated the Taira in the Genpei War, establishing the Kamakura shogunate.

name: Kamakura
summary: Japan's first military government, marking the rise of the samurai warrior class. Zen Buddhism, martial values and austere aesthetics shaped culture, though the court in Kyoto retained ceremonial authority.

fell.text: The Kamakura shogunate fell to imperial loyalist forces, though military rule continued under the Ashikaga.

name: Tibetan Empire
summary: A powerful Central Asian empire under Songtsen Gampo and his successors. Adopted Buddhism, created a writing system based on Indian scripts and competed with Tang China and the Arab Caliphate for control of the Silk Road.

fell.text: The assassination of the last emperor Langdarma triggered fragmentation into competing regional kingdoms.

name: Xiongnu
summary: The first great steppe empire under Modu Chanyu, controlling Mongolia and threatening Han China. Developed sophisticated cavalry tactics, metalworking and a dual administrative system for nomadic and settled peoples.

fell.text: The Xiongnu confederation fragmented under pressure from the Xianbei and Han Chinese forces.

name: Göktürk Khaganate
summary: The first Turkic empire to use the name Türk, controlling the Silk Road from Manchuria to the Black Sea. Created the first Turkic writing system on stone monuments and maintained complex relations with China, Persia and Byzantium.

fell.text: The Uyghur tribes defeated the Göktürks and established their own khaganate in 744.

name: Maurya
summary: India's first great empire under Chandragupta and Ashoka, controlling most of the subcontinent. Known for Ashoka's edicts promoting Buddhist ethics, sophisticated administration and monumental stone pillars.

fell.text: The last Maurya emperor was assassinated by his general Pushyamitra Shunga, who founded the Shunga dynasty.

name: Gupta
summary: India's golden age of science, mathematics, literature and art. Aryabhata's astronomy, the decimal system, Kalidasa's plays and exquisite temple architecture mark this classical period.

fell.text: The Gupta Empire fragmented under Huna invasions and internal pressures, leading to regional kingdoms.

name: Chola
summary: A maritime empire that dominated southern India and Southeast Asian trade. Famous for bronze sculptures, the Brihadisvara Temple and naval expeditions to Southeast Asia.

fell.text: The Chola dynasty declined and was absorbed by the Pandya kingdom in 1279.

name: Delhi Sultanate
summary: Five successive Muslim dynasties that ruled northern India, introducing Persian culture, Islamic architecture and new administrative systems. The Qutb Minar and other monuments reflect Indo-Islamic synthesis.

fell.text: Babur defeated the last Delhi Sultan at the Battle of Panipat in 1526, establishing the Mughal Empire.

name: Vijayanagara
summary: A Hindu empire that resisted Islamic expansion and fostered Dravidian architecture, literature and trade. The capital at Hampi became one of the world's largest cities before its destruction in 1565.

fell.text: After the disastrous Battle of Talikota in 1565, the empire gradually fragmented and disappeared by 1646.

name: Mughal
summary: One of the world's largest empires, known for the Taj Mahal, religious tolerance under Akbar, administrative reforms and Indo-Persian culture. The empire declined after Aurangzeb's death.

fell.text: The last Mughal emperor was exiled by the British after the 1857 Rebellion, ending formal Mughal rule.

name: Funan
summary: The earliest known kingdom in Southeast Asia, located in the Mekong delta. Indianized culture, maritime trade and early state formation mark this important polity, though details remain uncertain.

fell.text: Funan was absorbed by the rising Chenla kingdom around 550 CE.

name: Khmer
aliases: អាណាចក្រខ្មែរ
summary: The greatest empire in Southeast Asian history, controlling much of the mainland. Angkor Wat and other temple complexes, sophisticated hydraulic engineering and divine kingship characterize this civilization.

fell.text: The Siamese kingdom of Ayutthaya sacked Angkor in 1431, ending the empire.

name: Srivijaya
summary: A maritime Buddhist empire that controlled the Strait of Malacca and dominated Southeast Asian trade. Known for Buddhist scholarship, naval power and connections between India and China.

fell.text: The Javanese Majapahit Empire conquered Srivijaya's remaining territories in 1377.

name: Majapahit
summary: The last major Hindu-Buddhist empire in Indonesia, controlling much of the archipelago. Known for the Nagarakretagama poem, temple architecture and maritime trade networks.

fell.text: The Islamic Demak Sultanate conquered Majapahit's capital in 1527, ending the empire.

name: Pagan
summary: The first unified Burmese kingdom, famous for thousands of Buddhist temples and pagodas. Theravada Buddhism became established and Burmese culture developed under royal patronage.

fell.text: The Mongol invasions and internal fragmentation led to the kingdom's collapse around 1297.

name: Ayutthaya
summary: A major Southeast Asian power that controlled much of mainland Southeast Asia. Known for international trade, Buddhist culture and the divine kingship concept before falling to Burma.

fell.text: The Burmese sacked and destroyed Ayutthaya in 1767, though Siam was quickly reunified.

name: Kushan
summary: A Central Asian empire that facilitated Silk Road trade between Rome, China and India. Patronized Buddhism, created Gandharan art blending Greek and Indian styles and issued gold coinage.

fell.text: The Kushan Empire fragmented under pressure from the Gupta Empire and Sasanian Persia.

name: Parthian
summary: A major Iranian empire that rivaled Rome, controlling the Silk Road. Known for mounted archers, feudal administration and cultural synthesis of Iranian, Hellenistic and Mesopotamian traditions.

fell.text: Ardashir I defeated the last Parthian king and established the Sasanian Empire in 224 CE.

name: Sasanian
summary: The last pre-Islamic Iranian empire, rivaling Rome and Byzantium. Zoroastrian state religion, sophisticated bureaucracy, monumental architecture and cultural influence on the Islamic world.

fell.text: The Arab Muslim conquest destroyed the Sasanian Empire, with the last king killed in 651.

name: Safavid
summary: Established Twelver Shia Islam as Iran's state religion, creating modern Iranian identity. Known for Isfahan's architecture, carpet weaving, miniature painting and conflicts with the Ottoman Empire.

fell.text: Nader Shah deposed the last Safavid ruler and established the Afsharid dynasty in 1736.
